tagline: Online course platform: lessons, student access, and payments.
verdictSummary: A single-course sales-and-delivery site — a landing page, checkout, magic-link login, gated video lessons, progress tracking — is a real, contained weekend-plus build for one course. What doesn't come with it is Teachable's breadth: multiple courses, affiliates, certificates, upsells, and everything else that makes it a full course business platform rather than one product page.
coreLoopDIY: A landing page with checkout, magic-link login for buyers, and gated Markdown lessons with a per-student progress tracker.
whatYouLose: support for multiple courses and a catalog
whyPeopleStillPay: A course business needs checkout, access control, progress tracking, and support to all just work together — people pay to avoid stitching and maintaining that themselves.
notes: Course platforms are tempting to DIY because the core loop looks simple; the full business surface underneath is genuinely deep, which is why this lands at 'kinda' rather than 'yes'.
prompt:
Build a single-course sales-and-delivery site, scoped to exactly one course. Course content lives as Markdown files organized into modules and lessons, each optionally pointing at a video file. A public landing page shows the course outline and price, with a buy button going straight to a hosted checkout. A webhook from the payment processor marks the buyer's email as enrolled. Login is by magic link only — enter your email, receive a signed sign-in link — no passwords, no OAuth. Gate lesson pages by enrollment, and serve video through short-lived signed URLs so a direct link expires rather than staying shareable forever. Track progress with a mark-complete button per lesson and a progress bar per module, stored per student.

Do not build support for multiple courses, affiliates, certificates, upsells, or coupon logic — this sells and delivers exactly one course. Payment receipts come from the payment processor directly; don't build invoicing or tax logic yourself. Note plainly in the README that a small VPS handles a modest audience fine, but a real launch with a large audience needs dedicated video hosting, not files served off a general-purpose server.

faq.q: Can I import my existing Teachable course?
faq.a: The lesson content, largely yes — copy your videos and written material into the Markdown lesson structure. Student enrollment and progress history don't transfer, since they're tied to Teachable's own billing and tracking.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: The landing page and lesson viewer are both responsive, so browsing and watching work fine on a phone. There's no dedicated mobile app or offline video download.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Hosting, a domain, and a database, typically a few dollars a month, plus standard payment-processing fees on sales — no monthly platform fee beyond that until real video-hosting costs kick in at scale.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: Running more than one course as a real business. This build is genuinely good at selling and delivering a single course; the moment there's a second course, a coupon, or an affiliate to manage, you're back to building platform features by hand.
